Stellenbosch Police Failures

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Stellenbosch - a seemingly quiet and peaceful university town - has been rocked by a number of abductions and violent crime. In October last year, we brought you the story of a terrifying crime trend.

Unique Selling Point:
In the weeks since our story aired, we have uncovered failures to investigate violent muggings by the Stellenbosch police station. Not only that, the spate of abductions that we thought started in June, in fact started as far back as February last year. Tonight, we bring you the story of a town in crisis, as police fail to properly investigate cases from muggings to abductions.

Summary:
In October last year, we broadcast the story of a terrifying new trend in Stellenbosch - the abductions of university students. Since our story aired, we have been investigating why police were not thoroughly looking into these cases. And we uncovered that the spate of abductions started as far back as February. Just days before our story went to air, a Stellenbosch University student, 19 year old Jesse Mitchell was murdered. He was cycling home after working on a project with fellow students, and was attacked, robbed of his backpack and cellphone, and stabbed in the neck. Could his murder have been avoided?

Further information:
Sources contacted Carte Blanche to expose the lack of police investigations in cases - from muggings.. to abductions. In one case a violent mugging was registered at the police station in April, and closed the very next day. An investigating officer was never even allocated to the case. We explore just how deep the rot is, and what is being done to protect students. We interview the brother and mother of Jesse Mitchell, the police, the university, and the mother of a student abducted as far back as February. We also interview the aunt of Hannah Cornelius - a Stellenbosch student who was abducted, raped and murdered almost eight years ago. She believes Hannah died in vain. Hannah's tragic murder made international headlines, but in the years since then security for students has not improved. We also interview Ian Cameron, an activist turned politician, and chair of Parliament's portfolio committee on police.

Script:


NATSOUND (Clip of Hannah) “Hello, yes I know, I look disgusting. I’m sick. So shut up and listen”.
Music playing

VO 1 Fluent in French and an accomplished pianist… Hannah Cornelius was a 21 year old Stellenbosch University student who had her whole life ahead of her.

NATSOUND “Hope you liked” Video ends

VO 2 But, in the early hours of May the 27th 2017, her life was cut short.

VO 3 Hannah had offered fellow student Cheslin Marsh a lift home after a night out. CCTV footage captured her blue Citi golf arriving and parking outside his residence. It also recorded four men walking past the car where the two sat chatting. But, a few minutes later the men returned to the car.

VO 4 The two students were abducted by three of the men and driven off in Hannah’s car. Later, Hannah was raped and brutally murdered. Cheslin was savagely assaulted and left for dead, but survived.

VO 5 Hannah’s aunt, Eleanor Cornelius, believed back then that Hannah had been in the wrong place at the wrong time.

UPSOUND Eleanor Cornelius / Aunt:. And we saw the whole crime that occurred as opportunistic. Now, seven years later, we can see that this is now becoming a pattern.

VO 6 All four attackers were subsequently arrested and sentenced…

VO 7 The story of Hannah’s murder made international headlines…..and now, in more recent months, serious, senseless crime has returned to haunt this university town.

UPSOUND Michèle Mitchell / Jesse’s mother: Aaron was sobbing. So we knew something was really wrong. And then he just said Jesse’s dead.

VO 8 First year student, Jesse Mitchell was cycling home in the early hours of October the 16th last year when he was attacked for his backpack and cellphone. Stabbed in the neck, he died within minutes. His body was discovered by a security guard. (shots of cycling etc)

VO 9 Could Jesse’s tragic death have been avoided if proper attention had been paid to student safety after Hannah’s murder almost eight years ago?

VO 10 And while these crimes happened off campus, what responsibility does the University have in keeping its students safe?

CONFRONT NATSOUND Prof de Villiers: I don’t like that you hijacked me.
LOURENSA: We didn’t hijack you.
Prof de Villiers: It’s extremely rude.

FADE TO BLACK

LINK When we broadcast our first investigation in October last year, we knew about five abduction cases, a crime trend we thought had started in June. But, after our story aired, we received information that it had been going on for far longer than that. Our producer received a Facebook message from a mother whose eighteen year old son was abducted in February last year.

VOICE NOTE (reading out message): My son was mugged of his phone and abducted and choked out. By the grace of God after being driven around for an hour and enroute to Somerset West, he managed to jump out the car and escape. We were one of the lucky ones.

VO 11 The case was reported to police detailing what could be remembered - four men in a white or silver car had abducted him.

VO 12 The mother, who did not want to be identified, received an SMS from Stellenbosch police that included the name of the investigating officer and a number for Stellenbosch police station. Despite the severity of the crime and the promise of an investigation, the family was contacted by police just once. To date, no one has been arrested and the case has gone cold.

LINK: Let’s see if we can get hold of the investigating officer by dialling the number provided in the SMS. This is the number for the Stellenbosch police station. This certainly doesn’t inspire much confidence in the Stellenbosch police.

VO 13 In the five abduction cases that we featured in our first investigation, two involved ransom demands. In those cases, there were arrests. But, in the others there’s been no progress.

NATSOUND Jodi (from first story) His friends they were outside a pub …

VO 14 Jodi Aigner featured in our previous investigation. Her son was abducted late last year and yet the case has already been closed.

UPSOUND Jodi Aigner / Mother: Josh was abducted on the 8th of September and the SMS I received from Stellenbosch SAPS was on the 19th of November.

LOURENSA: Did you even receive so much as a phone call from the investigating officer?

UPSOUND Jodi Nothing, nothing, not Josh, not myself.

VO 15 Josh, a final year Stellenbosch university student was abducted outside a bar, in full view of his friends, and driven around for several hours before being released in neighbouring Cloetesville..

UPSOUND Lourensa: Was he able to tell the police what the car looked like or the people driving the car?
Jodi: He told them it was a white vehicle that had been used, he couldn’t remember the exact make. Not one of the witnesses that actually saw him were followed up with.

VO 16 For Debbie Lee, the mother of a Stellenbosch University student, it was clear crime in the town was escalating out of control. Unlike other universities in the country, Stellenbosch is an open campus intertwined with the town. And so while crimes were happening off campus, there is an obligation by the university to alert students in its care. It was only through whatsapp groups that Debbie began to realise just how bad the situation was.. Disturbingly, many cases were closed after just a few weeks, or in some cases only days.

UPSOUND Debbie Lee / Safer Stellenbosch Group: The moms who started it did a great job, I just rolled on it with it to see what could done to benefit the university, the kids, tourists to get a beautiful Stellenbosch again.

VO 17 Her phone lit up with case after case..

NATSOUND

UPSOUND Debbie Lee: It’s been kind of hair raising to see what has come past my way. And I’ve been desperately sorry for the kids. And I just feel like we need to do more.

VO 18 Debbie says she shared her database with the municipality two days before Jesse Mitchell was murdered. And she feels there’s still not enough collaboration.

VO 19 But, she’s determined to change that….By raising awareness and lobbying for improved security in the town. Her research has uncovered troubling crime patterns. Is it possible that the same car has been used in at least some of the incidents reported to her? Or perhaps it's a syndicate at work?

UPSOUND Debbie Lee / Mother Clip 477 Day 3 / Cam 1 Time code 02:36 I’m thinking it’s a syndicate, I’m not a police officer, just from what I’ve seen, what people have shared with me, what establishments have shared with me, there always seems to be a white car in the picture.

NATSOUND Cellphone footage of three girls (used in first story)

VO 20 After a night out on April the 25th last year, Jolene Mather and her two friends were walking home. Jolene filmed a white car following them. We featured their story back in October. But, in the weeks since then we were able to obtain the CCTV footage of the incident. In it - a white car is clearly visible - so is the face of one of the assailants. He saunters back to the car, clearly unconcerned about the possibility of being apprehended.

VO 21 And just two days later, another student was attacked in exactly the same way. She contacted our producer with details of her case, but wanted to remain anonymous. She had been walking home at 10 at night when a white car stopped next to her and a man jumped out of the car, chased her and stole her bag.

VO 22 She reported the case to police but the very next day she received an SMS to say the case had been closed.

ON SCREEN: I was extremely disappointed with the police’s lack of effort as a similar occurrence happened to my boyfriend only a month prior. His belongings were also stolen from him outside a popular pub in Stellenbosch by three men in a white car. I believe these were the same men.

VO 23 Several months after these incidents, this white car was captured in CCTV footage just before a student was attacked outside a restaurant.

UPSOUND Debbie Lee: It’s been very emotional to be honest to see what’s happened. Especially with Jesse Mitchell’s case. May he rest in peace. I knew with the trend, sorry I get emotional, I knew something was going to happen. Sorry.
LOURENSA: And then something did happen.
UPSOUND Debbie Lee Something did happen.

VO 24 The 16th of October was Jesse’s nineteeth birthday, but he would not get to celebrate. His girlfriend phoned his brother Aaron to break the news.

UPSOUND Aaron Mitchell / Jesse’s brother: He was riding his bike back to his apartment after a late night of computer science projects. And someone had stopped him, and he had been stabbed and they took his bag and his cellphone. He died there.

VO 25 Jesse’s mother Michele couldn’t get hold of him to wish him for his birthday.

UPSOUND Michèle Mitchell / Mother: Aaron was sobbing. So we knew something was really wrong. And then he just said Jesse’s dead.

UPSOUND Aaron Mitchell / Jesse’s brother: I was an absolute mess. I couldn’t believe it. I kept telling her. No this can’t be true. This can’t be real. It can’t be Jess. There’s no ways.

VO 26 Aaron will forever miss his brother’s laugh.

UPSOUND Aaron Mitchell 20:40 He’d walk into a room and you’d just feel this positive energy coming out of him. The room would just warm up. There will always be a scar with him gone.

VO 27 The street where Jesse was murdered is dimly lit. So are many others in this area. It’s ripe for criminality. And students are soft targets.

UPSOUND Aaron Mitchell / Jesse’s brother: I had no idea all of this was going on. I think if I had I would have sent him somewhere else, I think it would have pushed him to get his driver’s license a little bit faster so that least he’s got a car so he could drive around if doing late night projects and stuff.

LINK: After Jesse’s murder, thousands of students signed a petition demanding increased patrols, improved street lighting, and more collaboration between police, private security and the university.

UPSOUND Debbie Lee 05:12 As parents there’s only so much you can do, I wish I could have waved a wand and it didn’t happen.

VO 28 But, there is work being done to prevent such serious crimes from happening again. And Debbie’s database is helping. Gretha Groeneveld has a PHD in spatial crime research and has been using that data as well as information from private security and neighbourhood watches to do crime mapping.

NATSOUND Lourensa: There’s like a hotspot right?
Gretha: Ja you can basically see three. One behind Eikestad Mall, there’s one at the bottom of Victoria Street, there’s one here around Dorp street.

VO 29 Police release crime statistics on a quarterly basis but she says it’s not being utilised in the way it should be. She’s on a mission to create an alternative crime database to help solve the problem.

UPSOUND Gretha Groeneveld / Crime Mapper: So when we get data as the public, some of it is already three months old. And that’s not good enough.

LOURENSA 05:47 What kind of difference do you think it would make if we had that kind of reliable data?
UPSOUND Gretha Groeneveld: A huge, huge difference. You need to understand how big the problem is to be able to manage it. If you don’t have the data, how can you manage the problem.

NATSOUND

VO 30 For now, she’s created an app that allows security guards and members of the public to report crime incidents and this up to date information indicates current hotspots. Letting local security companies focus on these areas.

NATSOUND I would give this maps to them, so they know where to send their resources so it could be hugely helpful.

VO 31 Knowing where the hot spots are is one thing, getting police to patrol them quite another….as we discovered on a Wednesday night.

LINK: This is a known hotspot for crime, ranging from muggings, to now murder. It’s 9.30 pm and we’ve been in the area for hours. During this time we haven’t seen a single police van on patrol.

VO 32 Shortly after Jesse’s murder, Rudolf Hufke was arrested. He’s the same age as Jesse was, just nineteen.

VO 33 Hufke will be back in court at the end of this month to face charges of aggravated robbery and murder. He will be joined in the dock by a security guard, Cornelius Kruger, who faces a charge of theft. Both of them spent Christmas behind bars. They have not yet pleaded to the charges against them.

VO 34 While an arrest in Jesse’s case was swift, for many of the abduction cases and violent muggings we investigated the cases were simply closed.

VO 35 Perhaps if they’d been properly investigated, criminals would not have become more emboldened.

LINK: We spent weeks setting up an interview with the Western Cape police commissioner, Thembisile Patekile. But, the day before we were supposed to meet him at his office here, he abruptly cancelled.

VO 36 We needed answers, and approached anti crime activist turned politician Ian Cameron to see if he could provide them.

VO 37 As the chairperson of Parliament’s Portfolio committee on police, he was able to request feedback from the police on a number of the cases we had investigated.

LOURENSA Were you able to get answers from the police?
UPSOUND Ian Cameron: Unfortunately up until now there’s been no proper feedback. It indicates either a lack of will or there is another problem that I don’t know, but something is very wrong.

VO 38 He says cases should not be closed so quickly, and believes it's an indication of serious police failures.

UPSOUND Ian Cameron: The fact that they are being closed without adequate reason to do so tells me there is either a leadership problem or there is a deliberate effort not to have it function properly.

VO 39 He believes closing a case after just one day as in the case of the student mugged in April last year, is indicative of the inadequacies.

LOURENSA: 00:16 Was there any investigation done in that matter? (Clip 312)
UPSOUND Ian Cameron 00:19 In my opinion no, there is just no way it could have been completed that quickly unless they had some success which we know they didn’t.

VO 40 The police said they had detected concerning crime patterns in the Cape Winelands District and had developed operational interventions to contain the situation. They conceded that there is a shortage of detectives at Stellenbosch police station, but said efforts to bolster capacity are ongoing.

VO 41 Stellenbosch Municipality declined to do an on camera interview, but in a statement said it plans to develop special walkways with enhanced lighting and increased patrols. The first route will include Borcherd Street where Jesse Mitchell died, and will be named after him to honour his memory.

ON SCREEN: To address student safety specifically, recent positive discussions with Stellenbosch University and the Mayor-Rector Forum resulted in plans to develop special walkways with enhanced lighting, CCTV coverage, and increased patrols. The first such special route will include Borcherds Street, where student Jesse Mitchell tragically lost his life. To honour his memory and commitment to safety, and following discussions with his family, this route will be named after him.

VO 42 We requested an on camera interview with Stellenbosch University but our repeated requests were declined in favour of a written statement. But, an issue of such significant public interest demanded answers, and so we confronted the Vice Chancellor Wim de Villiers at a graduation ceremony in December last year. .
.
CONFRONT (Day 2 / Cam 1/ clip 392) 00:07 Prof de Villiers, Lourensa Eckard from Carte Blanche. Lourensa: Why will the university not talk to us?
01:00 I don’t like that you hijacked me. It’s very rude.
PROF: 01:44 I’m not worried at this stage. Security issue in the town. We have more than 1300 CCTV cameras. We have more than 200 campus security personnel.
LOURENSA: Do you think the police and municipality should do more?
Prof: No, I think they work well with us.
03:30 The problem is when people are off campus.
LOURENSA:Is your message to parents and students that Stellenbosch is a safe campus?
Prof: 03:40 Stellenbosch is an absolutely safe campus. I would send my own kids here any time.

VO 43 After this encounter the University shared its safety plan with us, assuring parents and students that steps are being taken to ensure a safe learning environment.

VO 44 But for Hannah Cornelius’s aunt, Eleanor, Stellenbosch will never again seem like a safe place.

UPSOUND Eleanor Cornelius 05:15 We thought she’s safe and the worst of the worst happened to her. And this now with the recent spate of incidents in Stellenbosch, people need to wake up. There is that duty of care on the University to warn students, to say to them these things are happening, I wonder if students know themselves.

VO 45 Losing Hannah resulted in complete devastation for the family. Her mother died just nine months later, her father two years ago, leaving only her brother.

UPSOUND Eleanor Cornelius / Hannah’s aunt: The son is autistic and doesn’t have the capacity to understand what happened to his family.

VO 46 Stellenbosch University says it has stepped up awareness campaigns, but for Jesse’s family it’s come too late… since his murder, they’ve had tattoos to honour his memory.

UPSOUND Michele Mitchell: Aaron, him and Jesse had a thing where you give it horns, so he had a horns tattoo, but were were laughing, because Jesse gave it horns this way which in sign language means I love you.

Our producer received a Facebook message from a mother whose eighteen year old son was abducted in February last year. VOICE NOTE (reading out message): My son was mugged of his phone and abducted and choked out. By the grace of God after being driven around for an hour and enroute to Somerset West, he managed to jump out the car and escape. We were one of the lucky ones. VO 11 The case was reported to police detailing what could be remembered - four men in a white or silver car had abducted him. VO 12 The mother, who did not want to be identified, received an SMS from Stellenbosch police that included the name of the investigating officer and a number for Stellenbosch police station. Despite the severity of the crime and the promise of an investigation, the family was contacted by police just once. To date, no one has been arrested and the case has gone cold. LINK: Let’s see if we can get hold of the investigating officer by dialling the number provided in the SMS. This is the number for the Stellenbosch police station. This certainly doesn’t inspire much confidence in the Stellenbosch police. VO 13 In the five abduction cases that we featured in our first investigation, two involved ransom demands. In those cases, there were arrests. But, in the others there’s been no progress. NATSOUND Jodi (from first story) His friends they were outside a pub … VO 14 Jodi Aigner featured in our previous investigation. Her son was abducted late last year and yet the case has already been closed. UPSOUND Jodi Aigner / Mother: Josh was abducted on the 8th of September and the SMS I received from Stellenbosch SAPS was on the 19th of November. LOURENSA: Did you even receive so much as a phone call from the investigating officer? UPSOUND Jodi Nothing, nothing, not Josh, not myself. VO 15 Josh, a final year Stellenbosch university student was abducted outside a bar, in full view of his friends, and driven around for several hours before being released in neighbouring Cloetesville.. UPSOUND Lourensa: Was he able to tell the police what the car looked like or the people driving the car? Jodi: He told them it was a white vehicle that had been used, he couldn’t remember the exact make. Not one of the witnesses that actually saw him were followed up with. VO 16 For Debbie Lee, the mother of a Stellenbosch University student, it was clear crime in the town was escalating out of control. Unlike other universities in the country, Stellenbosch is an open campus intertwined with the town. And so while crimes were happening off campus, there is an obligation by the university to alert students in its care. It was only through whatsapp groups that Debbie began to realise just how bad the situation was.. Disturbingly, many cases were closed after just a few weeks, or in some cases only days. UPSOUND Debbie Lee / Safer Stellenbosch Group: The moms who started it did a great job, I just rolled on it with it to see what could done to benefit the university, the kids, tourists to get a beautiful Stellenbosch again. VO 17 Her phone lit up with case after case.. NATSOUND UPSOUND Debbie Lee: It’s been kind of hair raising to see what has come past my way. And I’ve been desperately sorry for the kids. And I just feel like we need to do more. VO 18 Debbie says she shared her database with the municipality two days before Jesse Mitchell was murdered. And she feels there’s still not enough collaboration. VO 19 But, she’s determined to change that….By raising awareness and lobbying for improved security in the town. Her research has uncovered troubling crime patterns. Is it possible that the same car has been used in at least some of the incidents reported to her? Or perhaps it's a syndicate at work? UPSOUND Debbie Lee / Mother Clip 477 Day 3 / Cam 1 Time code 02:36 I’m thinking it’s a syndicate, I’m not a police officer, just from what I’ve seen, what people have shared with me, what establishments have shared with me, there always seems to be a white car in the picture. NATSOUND Cellphone footage of three girls (used in first story) VO 20 After a night out on April the 25th last year, Jolene Mather and her two friends were walking home. Jolene filmed a white car following them. We featured their story back in October. But, in the weeks since then we were able to obtain the CCTV footage of the incident. In it - a white car is clearly visible - so is the face of one of the assailants. He saunters back to the car, clearly unconcerned about the possibility of being apprehended. VO 21 And just two days later, another student was attacked in exactly the same way. She contacted our producer with details of her case, but wanted to remain anonymous. She had been walking home at 10 at night when a white car stopped next to her and a man jumped out of the car, chased her and stole her bag. VO 22 She reported the case to police but the very next day she received an SMS to say the case had been closed. ON SCREEN: I was extremely disappointed with the police’s lack of effort as a similar occurrence happened to my boyfriend only a month prior. His belongings were also stolen from him outside a popular pub in Stellenbosch by three men in a white car. I believe these were the same men. VO 23 Several months after these incidents, this white car was captured in CCTV footage just before a student was attacked outside a restaurant. UPSOUND Debbie Lee: It’s been very emotional to be honest to see what’s happened. Especially with Jesse Mitchell’s case. May he rest in peace. I knew with the trend, sorry I get emotional, I knew something was going to happen. Sorry. LOURENSA: And then something did happen. UPSOUND Debbie Lee Something did happen. VO 24 The 16th of October was Jesse’s nineteeth birthday, but he would not get to celebrate. His girlfriend phoned his brother Aaron to break the news. UPSOUND Aaron Mitchell / Jesse’s brother: He was riding his bike back to his apartment after a late night of computer science projects. And someone had stopped him, and he had been stabbed and they took his bag and his cellphone. He died there. VO 25 Jesse’s mother Michele couldn’t get hold of him to wish him for his birthday. UPSOUND Michèle Mitchell / Mother: Aaron was sobbing. So we knew something was really wrong. And then he just said Jesse’s dead. UPSOUND Aaron Mitchell / Jesse’s brother: I was an absolute mess. I couldn’t believe it. I kept telling her. No this can’t be true. This can’t be real. It can’t be Jess. There’s no ways. VO 26 Aaron will forever miss his brother’s laugh. UPSOUND Aaron Mitchell 20:40 He’d walk into a room and you’d just feel this positive energy coming out of him. The room would just warm up. There will always be a scar with him gone. VO 27 The street where Jesse was murdered is dimly lit. So are many others in this area. It’s ripe for criminality. And students are soft targets. UPSOUND Aaron Mitchell / Jesse’s brother: I had no idea all of this was going on. I think if I had I would have sent him somewhere else, I think it would have pushed him to get his driver’s license a little bit faster so that least he’s got a car so he could drive around if doing late night projects and stuff. LINK: After Jesse’s murder, thousands of students signed a petition demanding increased patrols, improved street lighting, and more collaboration between police, private security and the university. UPSOUND Debbie Lee 05:12 As parents there’s only so much you can do, I wish I could have waved a wand and it didn’t happen. VO 28 But, there is work being done to prevent such serious crimes from happening again. And Debbie’s database is helping. Gretha Groeneveld has a PHD in spatial crime research and has been using that data as well as information from private security and neighbourhood watches to do crime mapping. NATSOUND Lourensa: There’s like a hotspot right? Gretha: Ja you can basically see three. One behind Eikestad Mall, there’s one at the bottom of Victoria Street, there’s one here around Dorp street. VO 29 Police release crime statistics on a quarterly basis but she says it’s not being utilised in the way it should be. She’s on a mission to create an alternative crime database to help solve the problem. UPSOUND Gretha Groeneveld / Crime Mapper: So when we get data as the public, some of it is already three months old. And that’s not good enough. LOURENSA 05:47 What kind of difference do you think it would make if we had that kind of reliable data? UPSOUND Gretha Groeneveld: A huge, huge difference. You need to understand how big the problem is to be able to manage it. If you don’t have the data, how can you manage the problem. NATSOUND VO 30 For now, she’s created an app that allows security guards and members of the public to report crime incidents and this up to date information indicates current hotspots. Letting local security companies focus on these areas. NATSOUND I would give this maps to them, so they know where to send their resources so it could be hugely helpful. VO 31 Knowing where the hot spots are is one thing, getting police to patrol them quite another….as we discovered on a Wednesday night. LINK: This is a known hotspot for crime, ranging from muggings, to now murder. It’s 9.30 pm and we’ve been in the area for hours. During this time we haven’t seen a single police van on patrol. VO 32 Shortly after Jesse’s murder, Rudolf Hufke was arrested. He’s the same age as Jesse was, just nineteen. VO 33 Hufke will be back in court at the end of this month to face charges of aggravated robbery and murder. He will be joined in the dock by a security guard, Cornelius Kruger, who faces a charge of theft. Both of them spent Christmas behind bars. They have not yet pleaded to the charges against them. VO 34 While an arrest in Jesse’s case was swift, for many of the abduction cases and violent muggings we investigated the cases were simply closed. VO 35 Perhaps if they’d been properly investigated, criminals would not have become more emboldened. LINK: We spent weeks setting up an interview with the Western Cape police commissioner, Thembisile Patekile. But, the day before we were supposed to meet him at his office here, he abruptly cancelled. VO 36 We needed answers, and approached anti crime activist turned politician Ian Cameron to see if he could provide them. VO 37 As the chairperson of Parliament’s Portfolio committee on police, he was able to request feedback from the police on a number of the cases we had investigated. LOURENSA Were you able to get answers from the police? UPSOUND Ian Cameron: Unfortunately up until now there’s been no proper feedback. It indicates either a lack of will or there is another problem that I don’t know, but something is very wrong. VO 38 He says cases should not be closed so quickly, and believes it's an indication of serious police failures. UPSOUND Ian Cameron: The fact that they are being closed without adequate reason to do so tells me there is either a leadership problem or there is a deliberate effort not to have it function properly. VO 39 He believes closing a case after just one day as in the case of the student mugged in April last year, is indicative of the inadequacies. LOURENSA: 00:16 Was there any investigation done in that matter? (Clip 312) UPSOUND Ian Cameron 00:19 In my opinion no, there is just no way it could have been completed that quickly unless they had some success which we know they didn’t. VO 40 The police said they had detected concerning crime patterns in the Cape Winelands District and had developed operational interventions to contain the situation. They conceded that there is a shortage of detectives at Stellenbosch police station, but said efforts to bolster capacity are ongoing. VO 41 Stellenbosch Municipality declined to do an on camera interview, but in a statement said it plans to develop special walkways with enhanced lighting and increased patrols. The first route will include Borcherd Street where Jesse Mitchell died, and will be named after him to honour his memory. ON SCREEN: To address student safety specifically, recent positive discussions with Stellenbosch University and the Mayor-Rector Forum resulted in plans to develop special walkways with enhanced lighting, CCTV coverage, and increased patrols. The first such special route will include Borcherds Street, where student Jesse Mitchell tragically lost his life. To honour his memory and commitment to safety, and following discussions with his family, this route will be named after him. VO 42 We requested an on camera interview with Stellenbosch University but our repeated requests were declined in favour of a written statement. But, an issue of such significant public interest demanded answers, and so we confronted the Vice Chancellor Wim de Villiers at a graduation ceremony in December last year. . . CONFRONT (Day 2 / Cam 1/ clip 392) 00:07 Prof de Villiers, Lourensa Eckard from Carte Blanche. Lourensa: Why will the university not talk to us? 01:00 I don’t like that you hijacked me. It’s very rude. PROF: 01:44 I’m not worried at this stage. Security issue in the town. We have more than 1300 CCTV cameras. We have more than 200 campus security personnel. LOURENSA: Do you think the police and municipality should do more? Prof: No, I think they work well with us. 03:30 The problem is when people are off campus. LOURENSA:Is your message to parents and students that Stellenbosch is a safe campus? Prof: 03:40 Stellenbosch is an absolutely safe campus. I would send my own kids here any time. VO 43 After this encounter the University shared its safety plan with us, assuring parents and students that steps are being taken to ensure a safe learning environment. VO 44 But for Hannah Cornelius’s aunt, Eleanor, Stellenbosch will never again seem like a safe place. UPSOUND Eleanor Cornelius 05:15 We thought she’s safe and the worst of the worst happened to her. And this now with the recent spate of incidents in Stellenbosch, people need to wake up. There is that duty of care on the University to warn students, to say to them these things are happening, I wonder if students know themselves. VO 45 Losing Hannah resulted in complete devastation for the family. Her mother died just nine months later, her father two years ago, leaving only her brother. UPSOUND Eleanor Cornelius / Hannah’s aunt: The son is autistic and doesn’t have the capacity to understand what happened to his family. VO 46 Stellenbosch University says it has stepped up awareness campaigns, but for Jesse’s family it’s come too late… since his murder, they’ve had tattoos to honour his memory. UPSOUND Michele Mitchell: Aaron, him and Jesse had a thing where you give it horns, so he had a horns tattoo, but were were laughing, because Jesse gave it horns this way which in sign language means I love you.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Stellenbosch - a seemingly quiet and peaceful university town - has been rocked by a number of abductions and violent crime. In October last year, we brought you the story of a terrifying crime trend.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In the weeks since our story aired, we have uncovered failures to investigate violent muggings by the Stellenbosch police station. Not only that, the spate of abductions that we thought started in June, in fact started as far back as February last year. Tonight, we bring you the story of a town in crisis, as police fail to properly investigate cases from muggings to abductions.
metadata.Summary: In October last year, we broadcast the story of a terrifying new trend in Stellenbosch - the abductions of university students. Since our story aired, we have been investigating why police were not thoroughly looking into these cases. And we uncovered that the spate of abductions started as far back as February. Just days before our story went to air, a Stellenbosch University student, 19 year old Jesse Mitchell was murdered. He was cycling home after working on a project with fellow students, and was attacked, robbed of his backpack and cellphone, and stabbed in the neck. Could his murder have been avoided?
metadata.Further information: Sources contacted Carte Blanche to expose the lack of police investigations in cases - from muggings.. to abductions. In one case a violent mugging was registered at the police station in April, and closed the very next day. An investigating officer was never even allocated to the case. We explore just how deep the rot is, and what is being done to protect students. We interview the brother and mother of Jesse Mitchell, the police, the university, and the mother of a student abducted as far back as February. We also interview the aunt of Hannah Cornelius - a Stellenbosch student who was abducted, raped and murdered almost eight years ago. She believes Hannah died in vain. Hannah's tragic murder made international headlines, but in the years since then security for students has not improved. We also interview Ian Cameron, an activist turned politician, and chair of Parliament's portfolio committee on police.
